claiming the pin
PINOE = 0x00 (release every pad)
TXPIN = 0x00 (the LEVEL first...)
...and the idle level is set BEFORE the
pin is claimed. A first version wrote
SRV_DATA here instead of 0, on the reasoning
that the pin was about to go high anyway.
The consequence: the line stayed RELEASED -
so pulled HIGH by the board's pull-up - from
reset until the first pulse, and the first
pulse therefore had
no rising edge at all
The TB saw four rises and five falls and
correctly refused to call it five pulses.
The idle level of a timing protocol is part
of the protocol.
PINOE = 0x40 (claim exactly one pad)
the line is released, so it READS HIGH for a moment
This is the TB's "leading fall": the wire model
is a pull-up plus the pads, so a released pin
floats up. It is why the TB pairs each RISE with
the NEXT fall rather than with the j-th fall.
the firmware drives it LOW: the servo idle
position 0: 1 000 us, then a FULL 20 ms slot
TXPIN = SRV_DATA (0x40) - the pulse starts
PULSE 0 = 1 000.15 us high
requested 1 000 us,
datasheet band: 1 000 .. 2 000 us
dly1/dly2/dly3 on dmem[0] = 97, (n2,n3) = (2,152)
one outer step = 4*152 + 11 = 619 clocks = 10.3 us
The tables are FITTED by division and a small
search, not by trial and error: for a chosen
(n2,n3) the outer counter nearest the target is
a division, and keeping every entry inside 255
is the search.
TXPIN = 0x00 - the gap starts
rise 0 -> rise 1 =
this is the number the 50 Hz claim rests on
position 1: 1 500 us, and the frame period is MEASURED here
TXPIN = SRV_DATA (0x40)
PULSE 1 = 1 500.13 us high
requested 1 500 us,
TXPIN = 0x00
The frame period is measured across TWO
DIFFERENT pulse widths on purpose. A fixed gap
after each pulse would give 20.5 ms here and
21.0 ms at the next position - 49 Hz then
47.6 Hz - and every per-pulse WIDTH check would
still pass. This is the measurement that tells
a slot from a delay.
positions 2..4: the widths still have to be right
short sweep gaps - 2.5 ms each, not slots
TXPIN = SRV_DATA / 0x00, 3 x (pulse, gap)
(+0.10) then (short)\n
Each short gap still exceeds 1 000 us, and the
TB PRINTS them as "a short sweep gap, not a
frame" rather than reporting them as slots.
done
dmem[10] = 5
The firmware parks with the line LOW, and the
TB asserts the LAST recorded edge is a fall.
A firmware that parked high would leave the
servo held at full travel forever.
the tolerances, and why they are the ones they are
Bands the TB uses, and what each is protecting.
pulse width 1 000 .. 2 001 us the servo would ignore or saturate outside
vs requested +/- 30 us the sweep would not be a sweep
frame period 19 900 .. 20 100 us 49.5 .. 50.25 Hz - the motor hums outside
short gap > 1 000 us a short gap is still a gap, not a second pulse
PULSE_MAX_US is 2000 + 1, and the 1 is stated rather than hidden:
a
firmware that produced exactly 2000.0 us would otherwise sit ON the datasheet
ceiling, and a ceiling a program can land on exactly is a ceiling a rounding
error can push it over.
Why the frame period is a band and the pulse widths are checked against
the REQUEST. A frame period is two measured widths added together, so its
error is the sum of the two tables' fitting error - bounded at 0.25 us each by
the construction in the firmware header. A band is the honest shape of that
claim. The widths are compared against what the firmware was ASKED for, which
is a different and stronger statement: it pins the sweep, not just the band.
The five measured widths are all 0.10 to 0.15 us LONG, and that is systematic.
The delay routine's clock count is exact - the core
is single-cycle, so N instructions take exactly N clocks - and the residue is
the table entry's FITTING: the outer counter is a whole number of steps, so
each entry lands at or just above its target. A count that could land short as
easily as long would be a worse mechanism, because the datasheet's interesting
bound on this protocol is a MINIMUM.
